utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Yes. Would the witness make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pasic. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Good morning, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. May I introduce Blessing Ikemefuna, who is a British lawyer just awaiting her solicitor's training contract and who has been with my team now since February and is doing a wonderful job. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Pasic, before you commence your evidence, I must draw your attention to a certain rule of evidence that we have here at the International Tribunal, that is Rule 90(E). Under this Rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecution, or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and as a consequence you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question, but in that situation the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled under such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you, Mr. Pasic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand, but I hope we won't have these problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pasic. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, before we start with Mr. Pasic, at the end of the testimony of General Keserovic yesterday Dr. Karadzic offered his report into evidence. I don't believe the Chamber did anything about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll receive it into evidence. Shall we assign a number for that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3848, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Excellencies. Good morning to everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Pasic.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you for waiting, but this is not your first evidence, so you have probably gained that experience. We need to make breaks, and we have to speak slowly. Could you please tell us whether you provided a statement to my Defence team.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I provided a statement, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 1D9152 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please look at the screen in front of you. Do you see that statement on the screen?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you read the statement, and did you sign it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown the last page. I would like to ask him to identify his signature on it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does your statement clearly reflect what you said to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes. If I understood you properly, you're referring to the statement that I provided to your Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm asking about inaccuracies?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Save for some minor grammatical errors, there's nothing that would change the essence of my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put the same questions to you today, the same ones they put to you when you provided your statement, would your answers be the same in essence?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I would tell the truth, so that's that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this statement pursuant to Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. It will be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3849, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now I am going to read a short summary of Mr. Radomir Pasic's statement in English. [In English] Radomir Pasic was born on 22nd of July, 1961, in Cerovica municipality of Novi Grad, formerly Bosanski Novi. In July 1990, he became a member of the SDS, and in 1992 he was the president of the Crisis Staff of the Novi Grad, Bosanski Novi, municipality. After the first multi-party elections Mr. Pasic was elected as the president of the municipality of Bosanski Novi. In order to avoid armed conflicts in Novi Grad, talks with the SDA were held on a daily basis, including with the SDA president Izet Muhamedagic. Radomir Pasic received information that non-Serbian residents of Bosanski Novi were arming and preparing for war, and it was to the non-Serbs' advantage that Bosanski Novi was at the border of Croatia and Krajina, in Croatia now, where peace was kept by the UNPROFOR. Mr. Pasic obtained intelligence that the Muslims were buying weapons from Croatia and Krajina and possibly even through UNPROFOR as well. In addition, in February and March 1992, the Muslims had set up a check-point between Bosanska Krupa and Novi Grad. He saw that Muslim members of the SFRY were wearing uniforms and traditional Muslim red fezzes from the Turkish time. Later, six trucks with Serb drivers were seized. On 4th of May, 1992, as the situation was becoming more complex, talks were held with the SDA, agreeing that all individuals, regardless of their ethnicity, hand in all held illegally weapons in order to protect peace and security of the citizens and the area. Though the Muslim representatives accepted this, it was not enforced. The weapons remained with the Muslim individuals and groups. In order to hand in illegally possessed weapons to the municipal Territorial Defence Staff or SJB by 11th of May, 1992, was issued by the ARK organs. Proceeding -- proceedings would be brought against those who failed to comply. Nevertheless, many, in particular the Muslims, ignored this order. Many weapons were found later in their houses. After finding that certain groups and individuals were possessing weapons illegally, the SJB and military police required facilities to take their statements and for surveillance. Due to the limited space in the SJB, the Mlakve stadium was used as a reception centre. People who were not dangerous were released, while some were kept in for the purpose of filing criminal report and investigation. In order to help and protect all the citizens and peace in Bosanski Novi, Radomir Pasic considered the best possible option was to enable Muslim citizens who wished to leave Bosanski Novi to do so. The non-Serbs wanted to leave only -- not only just for political and security reasons but also social and economic concerns such as to be reunited with family members abroad, and the difficult situation in the municipality, for example, shortage of food, water, and electricity. Radomir Pasic explained this to Charles Kirudja, the representative from UNPROFOR, and asked him to assist these people for a safe and peaceful passage through the territory of the Republika Srpska Krajina. Furthermore, those who decided to leave Novi Grad voluntarily were able, if they wished, to take with them all their personal property, including passenger cars and cargo vehicles. With regard to real estate, they could sell it, swap it, or give it away without any duress for the municipality authorities. Regarding the paramilitaries, Radomir Pasic knew they were operating in Bosanski Novi. However, they were not invited by the authorities, and he was asked to remove them from the territory of the municipality. Radomir Pasic said he was aware that some mosques were destroyed but was unaware of the identity of the perpetrators. And that's the summary, and at that moment I do not have additional questions for Mr. Pasic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Pasic, as you have noted, your evidence in chief in this case has been admitted in its entirety in writing, that is via your written statement in lieu of your oral testimony, and now you will be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I remain seated for -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By all means, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Pasic. Mr. Pasic, do you hear me? You're nodding your head. You need to affirmatively answer so that your answer is on the record.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, that's the speed in which you should proceed. There's a gap due to the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, you say in your statement that you had no information about the establishment of the Serbian municipal assemblies in the municipalities of Bosnia-Herzegovina or about the proclamation of same, and when you were asked to describe information you have about the reasons for the establishment and operation of Serbian Crisis Staffs in the municipalities, you simply said that you have already pointed out in the statement that there were reasons to establish a system to maintain peace and security of citizens. Firstly, you had information at the time about the establishment of Serbian Municipal Assemblies and of Serbian Crisis Staffs, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: If I understood you properly, I don't know what you mean when you say Serbian municipality. I can talk about Novi Grad municipality, and I know that in that municipality, as you could see from my statement, there was a certain percentage of all the ethnicities. So we didn't have that kind of problem in Novi Grad municipality. In other words the division of powers was --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] stop you there. If I can just interrupt you there. You say that you have no information about the establishment of Serbian municipalities, Municipal Assemblies. You testified in the Krajisnik trial in December 2005 and January 2006. In that trial you admitted being aware of the December 1991 instructions from the SDS Main Board, also referred to as the Variant A and B document, and you said in your interview when you were interviewed by members of the Office of the Prosecutor, which was on the 13th of June, 2003, that you think you received the instructions but you claim you don't remember where you got it from. So you are aware of this document, are you not?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, but that is not a question that you asked me before. You asked me about Serbian municipalities. I'm familiar with Variants A and B, but I didn't understand what you asked me before.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, that document talks about the establishment of Serbian Municipal Assemblies and also about establishing Crisis Staffs, and as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Why don't you try to resolve the translation issue. The question was about whether you had information about the establishment of Serbian Municipal Assemblies and Serbian Crisis Staffs. Now do you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I thought we were talking in plurals, and I can only speak about Bosanski Novi Municipal Assembly or Novi Grad municipality, as I testified in the Krajisnik case. I can repeat those words again, perhaps not fully. I said that I was familiar with the Variants A and B but those were not about the establishment of Serbian Municipal Assemblies. As far as I can remember, those were some instructions or suggestions as to how to react to some unwanted consequences if those should arise. I believe that that's -- that was the gist of that document. There was no reference to the establishment of Serbian Municipal Assemblies. Where Serbian population was a minority and where Serbian population was a majority, those were two -- the two variants according to which people were supposed to behave, and that was the gist of the document as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be instructed to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you speak more slowly for the benefit of the interpreters and us. Back to you, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, Bosanski Novi was a Variant A municipality, wasn't it, because it had the majority of Serbs?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Or -- the municipal president you made sure that the December 1991 instructions were implemented in Bosanski Novi, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: When I received those instructions, as I've already testified, I don't remember when they arrived and how they arrived. There is no doubt about the fact that we did receive those instructions, and I must admit that there was some dead-lines there, but we missed some of them with regard to those activities because in Bosanski Novi, which is now Novi Grad, there was no need really for any additional instructions because the authorities functioned normally. Muslims participated, and in those terms those instructions were of not much use, if I may put it that way, because we acted even without those instructions, obviously in keeping with the provisions of the constitution of the state where we lived at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, do you agree that line 23 of previous page should read "Bosanski Novi was a Variant A municipality," not "Variant A and B"?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, in the report on the work of the Bosanski Novi Crisis Staff -- you know the document that I'm referring to, don't you? This is Exhibit P2632 in this case. You said in its original form the municipal Crisis Staff was formed at the beginning of April by the Municipal Board of the Serbian Democratic Party on the proposal and according to instructs of higher organs of the SDS party. So you -- you did form this municipal Crisis Staff, and you acted according to these instructions that we've just been discussing, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes. Sometime in the month of April, I don't know the exact date but it was in 1992 in any case. That Crisis Staff was established officially, and it became operational at that time. However, according to those instructions, our Crisis Staff should have been set up even before that. However, I did not feel the need to establish a Crisis Staff, as I've already told you. A Crisis Staff is a constitutional category, and it was provided for in the constitution of the then Socialist Federative Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In an immediate threat the war or in situations when legal bodies of local community could not be called, a Crisis Staff was supposed to take over their role and to operate under those circumstances. Since the situation in Bosanski Novo before then was relatively calm, in other words, conflicts had not escalated, there was no shooting, there were no armed activities, although in 1991 Croatian Army did attack the territory of Bosanski Novi. However --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] Mr. Pasic, can I interrupt you --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: -- during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- you're getting -- you're getting far away from -- from my question. This Court's heard quite a bit of evidence that there was an extended session of the deputy's club on the 14th of February, 1992, at which Dr. Karadzic activated the second degree of Variant A and B. Now, you were registered at the Holiday Inn where that meeting was held, were you not?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: I wanted to clarify the role of a Crisis Staff and why and when the Crisis Staff was set up in Bosanski Novo. You interrupted me but that's your problem. I was at Holiday Inn once but I don't remember that on that occasion when I was there there were discussions about Variants A and B. I already said that once when I was here. I was given a receipt for accommodation at that hotel, but I don't remember that I received that receipt before, so I don't understand it when you put it to me that I participated in the drafting of some documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, I didn't put that to you. I simply asked you if you were registered at the Holiday Inn where the meeting was held. The receipt, as you say, which was shown to you in the Krajisnik case was a receipt for both in your name and Mr. Dejanovic's name. There were two Dejanovics in the SDS in -- in Bosanski Novi, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes. If we are speaking in the masculine, then there were two Dejanovics who were in the Serbian Democratic Party at the time, but I am not aware of having slept with any one of them. If it were a woman, perhaps it would have been different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me intervene here. Ms. Sutherland, if you want the witness to answer simply, you need to put the question simply. I read your question again, and then you said there was an extended session of the deputies' club on the 4th of February at which Dr. Karadzic activated the second degree of Variant A and B, so the witness is fair enough to commented on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I take your point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, when you -- when you testified in the Krajisnik case, in fact, you said just a moment ago that you -- you don't remember sharing a room with Mr. Dejanovic, and you couldn't remember Mr. Karadzic discussing this second level -- activating the second level. In fact, he mentioned it on no less than four occasions in that extended session that you -- that you say that you don't recall attending. Is that -- is that still your -- you evidence that you -- that you don't recall attending this meeting?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Well, I really cannot assert anything. First of all, later on I saw some documents, and if we are talking about the same document, let's call it Variant A and B, it seems to me that it's sometime in December 1991 that it was passed, so I said that I did not attend that session. Now, whether I attended some other session where probably there was some discussion with regard to these activities, I really don't know. I really cannot remember. However, what I can assert is that I never slept in the Holiday Inn with any one of the Dejanovics.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'll move on. Mr. Pasic, in the report on the work of the Crisis Staff, you make reference to the implementation of the government's decision on disarming during the time period the 5th to the 11th of May, and in your statement you refer to a 4 May 1992 ARK decision in -- it's in paragraph 10 of your statement. You're aware that this ARK decision, which is Exhibit P02418 was issued pursuant to a republic level order from General Subotic which is P02818, yes?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, you asked me whether this was in keeping with some republican decree?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. Are you aware that this ARK decision was issued pursuant to a republic level order from General Subotic? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Well, at the time I think I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: I know that a decision arrived from Krajina, an order arrived, and it was accepted in the sense of trying to establish some kind of peace, because there was increasing danger coming from these groups, military formations. I'm referring to both ethnic communities. I accepted that as a solution to establish public law and order. As for the relations between the AR Krajina and the republican organs, at least at that point in time I was not aware of this being sent from the very top or ordered.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The fact of the matter is you were only disarming the Muslim population, were you not?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. There are many written records, many documents showing the action that we were involved in; namely that all paramilitary formations be placed under the command of the then staff of the Territorial Defence as it was formulated in the former Yugoslavia, and later on it was the organisation of the Army of Republika Srpska. Actually, first it was the Army of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, later on Republika Srpska. I can even give you some examples.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: We as the authorities --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry, I want to interrupt you there. You said that -- but by definition then, anyone who -- who doesn't join the TO is a paramilitary if a person owns a weapon; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Well, of course everything that is outside the institutions of a system of a state is unlawful, that is to say any illegal keeping of weapons by anyone is illegal and unlawful. We were aware that a large number of people had weapons. I'm talking about the municipality of Bosanski Novi, Novi Grad. We embarked upon this activity, and on the basis of the decision that you mentioned, and we tried up until the 10th or 11th of May to deal with this in a normal way, that all of these weapons of paramilitaries irrespective of ethnicity be placed under the control of the staff of the TO or the civilian police. That was the objective because --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, the settlements named in the last paragraph of paragraph 12 of your statement are all Muslim settlements, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: There's no mention in your statement of -- of any Serb villages that -- that were searched for weapons?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: This is a question that would indeed require a lengthy answer. However, you keep interrupting me, so I'm not in a position to complete my thoughts and therefore you cannot understand my answers. If you allow me, I shall try to respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have say that in that period -- actually, we'd have to go back a bit. There was a generally difficult situation throughout the former Yugoslavia. The winds of war had already started blowing from Slovenia and Croatia. Bosanski Novi is on the very border with Croatia or, rather, the then-Serb Republic of the Krajina. We had a series of problems, even with small groups that were of Serb ethnicity that unfortunately came from Dvor na Uni which is a municipality on the other side of the border in Croatia, that is to say the Krajina. We had a huge number of Serb refugees who used to live in Croatia before that, in Zagreb and other Croatian cities, so the situation was becoming evermore complex. In Bosanski Novi, now that you've asked me whether we disarmed the Serb population as well, I have to point out that the Serb population did not feel that kind of need, not to that extent, as was probably felt. I don't know what the motives were, fear of war or something else. Like the Muslim population, the Serb population did not feel that they should arm themselves to that extent so they were seeking some kind of salvation, protection through legal institutions, lawful institutions like the police, the Territorial Defence Staff. Unfortunately, most of the Muslim population refused mobilisation as far as military formations are concerned, legal military formations. They refused mobilisation. They refused to work at the police station, although we asked them to. We beseeched them, and we pointed out that it was dangerous, because if they excluded themselves from the legal organs there would be a lack of security felt among the civilian population, and there would be chaos. And then the civilian population of Muslim ethnicity would not feel safe as far as the legal organs were concerned. So I believe this is a mistake. I believe this is a mistake precisely on the part of these persons who avoided legal organs in the local commune like the TO staff, like the public security station, and they avoided working in these institutions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: And then of course the situation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Continue, but if you could be more succinct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. It is hard to explain this in two words only. I wish to say that unfortunately the situation was that the Muslim population was avoiding institutions and organs that existed, and that was a guarantee. And these people as they were avoiding this obligation of theirs, if you will, indirectly placed themselves in that position, and a large number of persons were arming themselves illegally, and that was why this attempt was made to put all of this within the framework of legal organs. I repeat, this is not only in these villages that are mentioned but wherever it was learned that there were such persons an attempt was made to disarm them. You interrupted me when I was answering the last question, too, but I can tell you something else. We also had some very unpleasant situations when a person of Serb ethnic background was physically liquidated because of disobedience vis-a-vis the legal institutions like the police, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, that's unnecessary. If you could focus on answering the question. Yes, please continue, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, just to pick up on something that you said on your answer when you were giving that -- that lengthy answer a moment ago, you said that the Serb population did not feel that they should arm themselves. You -- you, in fact, were involved in the arming of the Serb population in Bosanski Novi, were you not?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: You mean whether I was personally involved in that?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, you were personally involved.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Well, no. That was not my role, and that was not the role of the Crisis Staff. Actually, there was no need. There were legal institutions like the TO staff that had legal weapons, and therefore I don't see any point.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Why would I be doing that when --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, if we can have a look at D01913.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, this is a -- a document that was seized from the -- from Banja Luka CSB, and if we look at the last paragraph on the last page of the document, on the third page of the document in English and page 3 of the B/C/S -- first of all, the document is talking about a review of the security relevant information for Bosanski Novi municipality, and it says here citizens of Serbian ethnicity are organised within the system of Territorial Defence mainly through the efforts of Radomir Pasic, president of the Bosanski Novi Municipal Assembly. So far about 1.300 Serbs have been armed mostly with automatic infantry weapons and they control a considerable amount of equipment for POB which is an anti-armour combat 90-millimetre -- 90-millimetre launchers, 176 MM ZiS gun and a small amount of 82- and 120-millimetre mortars. So that's contrary to what you just asserted, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: No. First of all, I don't know whose document this is. In my view it doesn't really matter. I repeat, as far as the arming of the TO staff is concerned, no additional efforts were required, so I don't see what kind of role I could be playing in some kind of arming as referred to in this information that you mentioned just now. I mean, really, I don't know how this was conceived of. When I was president of the Municipal Assembly and by May president of the Crisis Staff, how could I affect not only the arming of the Serb population as mentioned here, it turns out that these were some sort of paramilitaries, but this was not what happened in practice, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Pasic, the JNA and the SDS were arming Serb volunteers in the Bosanski Novi municipality, weren't they? And you were aware of the JNA arming Serbs there, and you said as much in -- in the Krajisnik trial when you testified, when you were shown what is Exhibit P00979 in our case, which is a report from General Kukanjac dated the 20th of March, 1992, and it's a document that evaluates the military situation in Bosnia and refers to the distribution of arms by the JNA and the SDS, and in the attachment it states that Bosanski Novi, there were 1.000 Serb volunteers that were armed. And what you said in the Krajisnik case was that you were aware that they were being unofficially armed by the JNA, and that was at transcript page 19730 to 19733. Now, recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether the translation is right or whether you mischaracterised my statement. As far as I can remember, I had stated that unfortunately through some channels that I believed were secret ones both ethnic communities were arming themselves. I'm referring to Serbs and Muslims, because there weren't any Croats in the municipality of Bosanski Novi. Very few were there, less than 1 per cent. So as for this indicia, I think that people from the former JNA were arming themselves. Where there where officers who were ethnic Serbs, I assume that they were arming Serbs, and over there where there were Muslims, I believe they were arming Muslims. But I believe that through different channels weapons were being brought in, and in this secret arming it was the Muslims that felt they had a greater need to do that because they had opted not to take part in the TO and the public security station and other lawful institutions and therefore they probably wanted to set up their own parallel institutions and units. I repeat, I'm not going say that the Serb population were not armed. There certainly were weapons there, too, but not to such a degree. There was not so much illegal weaponry, because they felt this feeling of safety and security because of these legal institutions. I have already said that. So this is a lesser degree of illegal weapons among the Serb population in Bosanski Novi. That's why I believe that because there were these legal formations there weren't so many illegal weapons, and I don't see what I as president of the Municipal Assembly was supposed to do by way of intervention when normally certain weapons existed in accordance with the system of the then-Yugoslavia and all municipalities had TO staffs. That's what it was called, the Territorial Defence. That is to say in the territory --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us clarify one thing, Mr. Pasic. You said in your testimony that there was not so much illegal weaponry. So you admit that then there were arming of legal institutions in your view?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I've already said if we take into account that the former Yugoslavia, that is to say the JNA, was there and some officers, some of Serb ethnicity and others of Muslim ethnicity, I'm not saying that this was legal arming, but I'm saying that this was one of the methods how people were arming themselves, through certain secret channels the officers of the then army gave certain people certain weapons. That's one of the ways in which this was done and then there was this other way, weapons were being bought. And I mentioned in Croatia a war was already underway by then, and I said that these were not classical state borders between Croatia and Bosnia, and it was very difficult to -- or, rather, it was not difficult to smuggle weapons and military equipment across these borders. As a matter of fact, according to some information the Serb population from the territory of Banja was selling military weapons to the Muslim population. That was a problem for Bosanski Novi. I said that this is a rather special municipality as compared to some of the central municipalities in then Bosnia-Herzegovina. The problem of the border, the problem of the war in Croatia, smuggled weapons through secret channels so both could arm themselves in that way. I was just trying to explain this. This is my personal position, my personal view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me put it this way --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thought that the Serb population had less of a need to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me put -- put a question this way: Take a look at the document which is before you, which is one of the Defence exhibits, D1913. Ms. Sutherland read out the paragraph: "Citizens of Serbian ethnicity are organised within the system of TO mainly through the efforts of Radomir Pasic, president of the Bosanski Novi Municipal Assembly. So far about 1.300 Serbs have been armed, mostly with automatic infantry weapons." I'll stop there. So these 1.300 Serbs could be referring to the members of the TO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I repeat once again that I really don't know who it was who wrote this document and what it was supposed to be in relation to myself. If it is my merit, then it is true that I insisted that the TO staff be manned according to mobilisation if that is my merit. I repeat, I don't know how many people were armed, and I must say that on the TO staff, well, I cannot say exactly by what time, but even the commanders included some Muslims and then they were leaving one by one, but one of them actually stayed on. Now, how many people were armed? How many people were placed under some kind of command and control of the TO staff? Only Serbs. I really don't know. I really don't have that information. And on the basis of what these 1.300 Serbs were referred to, I don't know how come. I don't know where this information came from. Did it come from certain units, battalions, brigades, something like that? I really don't know. If I understood your question correctly, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Back to you, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I omitted to say when I had no objection to the statement being tendered by the Defence that I would be seeking additional time to deal with a number of matters that are contained within the new 20 paragraphs that we were provided with in the early hours of Saturday morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You have already two hours, but let's see how it evolves at the [overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I just wanted to alert you to the fact that I -- I think I would be needing approximately another 45 minutes to deal with at least 10 of the 22 adjudicated facts that Mr. Pasic deals with in his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, paragraph 20 -- 47 of your statement deals with adjudicated fact 2283, and that concerns around the 9th of May, 1992, the Bosanski Novi Crisis Staff under Radomir Pasic issued an ultimatum over Bosanski Novi radio for Muslims in the municipality to hand in their weapons within 24 hours. And you stated that no such order existed and it never sought to disarm only one nation. I just want to take you to -- read some testimony of Mr. Midho Alic, who testified in the Krajisnik trial at transcript page 2590 where he's asked and said: "They said that the Muslims Bosniaks should surrender their weapons. That was the -- that was what the announcement said." And so there's a question: "So the actual announcement said it wasn't just because your village was only populated by Muslim, Blagaj Rajpa -- Japra," sorry. And his answer was: "No, it was not only on the radio, it was Ranko Grozdjen [phoen] who told me that. His story was the same that Muslims should surrender their weapons. "Q. All right. So you're saying it didn't apply to everybody. "A. No, it didn't. "Q. And this particular radio station you're talking about, to your knowledge are you aware to whom that particular radio station broadcast? "A. It broadcast to everybody, Muslims, Serbs, Croats. Everyone could listen to this radio station." The Crisis Staff used the radio to make announcements, didn't it? You said -- you said as much in your Crisis Staff report that the utmost use of the Bosanski radio should be made.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Well, radio Bosanski Novi is a local radio station which broadcast all information, and often the Crisis Staff also made declarations on the radio, but as I said, the point was to disarm all paramilitaries irrespective of their ethnic affiliation. The statement of the witness that you quoted may or may not have been competent to speak about these things. I don't know that person. The name is not familiar, so I cannot tell. But certainly it's a subjective assessment of his.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Pasic, is the name Miroslav Vjestica, is that familiar to you? Yes or no? Do -- do -- are you familiar with Vjestica from Bosanska Krupa, a neighbouring municipality?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know the name Miroslav Vjestica but not Miroslav Ristic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: There must have been a mistranslation. I -- I said Vjestica. I must have not spoken clearly. This is what he said on the 12th of May, 1992, at the 16th Assembly session. He said: As for Bosanski Novi, let me tell you -- and this is at page 21 of the English translation and B/C/S page 17. As for Bosanski Novi, let me tell you that I was there yesterday. Bosanski Novi is sealed off. An ultimatum has been issued and a dead-line set for the Muslims to surrender their weapons. Some of them did, some did not. Yesterday there was shooting. What will happen today? I believe they will surrender. The same is going on in Sanski Most. I think that the Muslims will soon be disarmed there too. So that's the case, isn't it, that -- that you were disarming the Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: I don't know what Mr. Miroslav Vjestica has said and in what capacity. For one thing he isn't from the Bosanski Novi municipality at all, if we are speaking about the same man. He is from Bosanska Krupa. He lived up there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] Mr. Pasic, he said I was there yesterday. He said, I said I visited Bosanski Novi yesterday, i.e., the 11th of May, so he has some personal knowledge of what he's talking about.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: I can only repeat that I cannot speak for anyone else. I don't know what he said and in what context he was and who he visited and what. Bosanski Novi is a large place. It isn't just a spot. It is not one office, it's a whole municipality, and where he was and with whom, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, once the Muslims have been disarmed so that they couldn't defend themselves, the Muslim villages were attacked. In -- in paragraphs 49, 50, and 51 of your statement this relates to adjudicated facts concerning the shelling of villages of Blagaj Rijeka, and Blagaj Japra. And if I can -- if I can just say in relation to paragraph 48, there's a mistake in the adjudicated fact. It said adjudicated fact 2283 and in fact it should be adjudicated fact 2279. And in paragraph 49, also another mistake. It talks about adjudicated fact 2283 again and it should be adjudicated fact 658. And in paragraph 51, it talks about adjudicated fact 2284 and it should be 2290, and I apologise for not alerting the Defence to that when they were tendering the statement or -- or before. But in any event, if we can go back to these facts. In fact, looking at paragraph 50, you say in the days following the 9th of May, 1992 -- this is the adjudicated fact: "In the days following 9 May 1992 Serb forces launched an attack on Blago Japra using heavy artillery which had been positioned around the village beforehand. Shells were fired into the village for two days and JNA soldiers shot and wounded civilians." And you said JNA did not officially exist in that period, and as far as I can remember on 12th of May, 1992, the Army of Republika Srpska of Bosnia-Herzegovina was officially formed. So the former staff TO reformulated to the Army RS BiH. I have already previous stated that there was not shelling --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry. I'm lost, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you break down your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is Mr. Pasic's response. This is in paragraph 50, the second paragraph to paragraph 50. He's responding to the adjudicated fact that's put to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So let's -- do you have your statement with you, Mr. Pasic? Does the Defence have a copy of his statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: We can put -- we can put it up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If the usher could assist.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: His statement is Exhibit D3849, and it's on page 20, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It's on page 16 of the B/C/S. And halfway through that second paragraph of paragraph 50 you say: There was no shelling except -- exceptionally in the places where there was resistance, and I think that our weapon carried -- and I think that that weapon carried -- kind of shelling but heavy artillery as far as I ever known did not exist. So it's your testimony that there was no shelling of -- of Blagaj Japra in May 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: I was a private in the army, and possibly we differ in terminology when we speak about shelling, but as a layman I know that there is light artillery and heavy artillery. So I may be wrong speaking in layman's terms, but when I spoke about the light weaponry or heavy artillery, when I said the latter I meant heavy howitzers, guns, tanks, so larger armaments. I wanted to say that the TO staff didn't have such weapons. There were light weapons, though, such as hand-held launchers, mortars of small calibres. If you meant that when you said artillery, maybe, but I explained giving my statement that I meant that there was light weaponry but no heavy weapons. And when I said that there was no shelling, I meant that there was no shelling from heavy howitzers, tanks, rocket launchers, and stuff. I'm not aware of any one village being shelled in that manner at that time. If we understand each other.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: May we go into closed session for a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry, private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Open session Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, do you recall that shelling --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask why we were in closed session if the witnesses were only mentioned by their codes -- code-names?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For that answer, we may have to go into private session again.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I think I can deal with it because they were -- they either testified in closed session or their statements were tendered under seal so what I was reading out as confidential information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic do you remember shelling lasting for seven days? Yes or no? Do you remember the shelling lasting for seven days? I -- we really have -- I have limited time --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is waiting for interpretation into B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat your answer, Mr. Pasic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that I cannot give a yes or no answer to such a long question. The Prosecutor made quite a long introduction.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, I was -- I was putting to you witness testimony about the shelling of Blagaj Japra and Blagaj Rijeka, and I said to you: Do you remember the shelling lasting for seven days. That was my question.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, but you put forward a number of facts to which I should reply before answering. We cannot skip them all.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, you've already said that in your view there were no heavy weapons used. I was --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Why -- why then ask me again? You put forward allegations that there were tanks with red, white, and blue flags. Red, white, and blue is the Croatian flag. I'm not aware of that happening. And there were no tanks at all, by the way. Or at least I didn't know that the Croatian Army had entered the Japra Valley.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Again I will ask you: Do you remember the shelling lasting for seven days?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: I have already stated, and I can repeat that I'm not aware of any heavy shelling, and I've given -- and I gave reasons. Whether there was shelling from light infantry weapons such as hand-held launchers and how long it went on I cannot say. And as for the duration of the operations, well, you can easily forget some things given how long ago it was --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, this was the --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: -- but there was some resistance in some villages to attempts at disarming the people.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] this -- this was -- this was the first heavy -- the first attack in the municipality, wasn't it? You would certainly remember that.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: The first attack officially happened at Blagaj when unknown perpetrators attacked a military police vehicle belonging to the TO staff. That was the first attack.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That was on the 10th of May, and that was when you then searched all these Muslim villages for weapons; correct? That was one incident where an unknown person fired at a -- at a-- on the road between Novi and Banja Luka -- Prijedor, sorry.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Well, you are --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm talking about an attack. I'm talking about Blagaj. That was first heavy attack in the municipality, was it not?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: I said that the first attack happened in the night of the 10th of May when the military police of the TO staff was attacked, and as far as I know, the perpetrators were unknown. I don't know if there was one or more perpetrators. You said that there was one, I believe, so you seem to have information that I don't have.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, could you hear the shelling?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: No. Since where I lived in my family house which is some 15 kilometres or more away, when that happened I got information over the radio because we didn't have regular phones at the time. I got information from the TO staff that someone had shot at the military police at Blagaj and that the situation is unclear --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm talking about --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: -- that there is no certain information --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] that lasted over seven days. Did you not hear that? Did you not go to work in the municipal building in those seven days?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Well, if you're asking me about shelling and supposing that there was shelling in the Japra valley, it again depends on the calibre of weapons used. And some shooting could not be heard in the municipal building. So if there was shooting from infantry weapons or hand-held launchers, it was impossible to hear there because the distance is some 15 to 20 kilometres. It's a valley. It might be a good thing to look at it on a map here so we could see -- all of us could see for ourselves. So probably the walls would block the sound. If you are specifically asking me if I heard any shooting with my own ears my answer is no. Certainly there was some information from people saying that there was some operations underway and, yes, I did have such information. But I must point out once more that I don't know how long that operation went on. Was it six days, seven days, two days, I really cannot tell you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, DanCon could hear it from across the river. That's Exhibit P03818. On the 11th of May at 1600 hours they said: There were reports of heavy funs and machine gun fire, probably tank guns and 20-millimetres. And they saw two houses were burnt. And this is -- this is what the MUP reported. And if we could have 65 ter 07 -- sorry, 06737 on the screen, please. The document that's coming up, Mr. Pasic, is a report from the security services centre in Banja Luka to the Serbian Republic BiH MUP and to all Chief of Staffs, and it's dated the 12th of May, 1992. And it says there members -- members of the Muslim nationality put up a barricade in Blagaj village and members of the Bosanski Novi Territorial Defence carried out a mortar attack on the village. This is on page 2 of the English.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please get a verbatim quotation of the sentence in question about Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: "Members of the Bosanski Novi TO carried out a mortar attack on Blagaj village at 2100 hours." Mr. Pasic, your report on the work of the Crisis Staffs also mentions artillery fire during this attack. Do you remember that? And that's at the bottom of page 4, the top of page 5 of your report. That's P02632.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: I don't know if there are -- misunderstandings are due to the interpretation or -- when I said that I didn't hear shooting, I specifically meant the attack in the night of the 10th. I didn't hear that kind of attack because at that time I was in my house. Whether anybody heard, and you mention a certain Mr. DanCon and where he was and where he heard it and when, I really don't know. So we're talking about some dates but we obviously don't understanding each other, at least it was not put clearly enough to me in the interpretation. If you have solid information, then please give it to me, which day, which hour, and so on. If I remember, I will tell you, but don't put hypothetical things to me in a period of 10 or 15 or 50 days because the situation changed from minute to minute.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Mr. Pasic --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Though if -- I would kindly ask you to specifically tell me which shelling you mean and which date and at what hour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm talking about the shelling that started on the 11th of May, 1992, and continued for seven days. The DanCon that I mentioned a moment ago - I'm sorry for giving you the acronym, I thought that you may be familiar - it's the Danish contingent which was across the River Una. But I will put -- I won't be putting anything hypothetical to you. I put it to you that the attack on Blagaj was on your orders.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: You obviously are not familiar with the role of the president of the Municipal Assembly, and I could speak at length about that. The president of the Municipal Assembly or the president of the Crisis Staff never had the authority to issue such orders. Consequently I didn't issue one, I couldn't. I didn't have the authority to do so to activate or disactivate anything in the military sense. The whole organisation of command along military lines is such. When the military police were attacked, I don't know who but someone from the TO staff must have reacted to that action. So there was a reaction to the attack on the military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Just --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: I was informed after that. I went to the TO staff -- you're interrupting me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I am interrupting you. You went to the TO staff. Is it your position you didn't order the shelling of Blagaj Japra? Just in a yes-or-no answer.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: I cannot answer that way. I have already stated my reasons.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You've just said about chain of command. You -- I just want you -- I want to be very clear about -- about your -- your testimony.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: No, you're not clear at all. We're speaking about shelling. Shelling is not such a clearly defined term. First you must tell me what you mean by shelling for me to be able to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you answer then whether you went to the TO staff and you ordered an attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, here it goes: Well, I was informed and went to the TO staff. Together with me the SDA president, Izet Muhamedagic, went there, and these actions were already underway. We only went there to get information about what had happened. I didn't issue any orders, and I couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] okay. You've answered the question. If I could have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let -- let us hear him out. Yes, continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I wanted to say that at that moment when we arrived at the TO staff we -- or, rather, I suggested that we invite Izet Muhamedagic who was president of the Municipal Board of the SDA party because I considered him to be a man of good reputation among the Muslims to see why that attack had happened and try to prevent an escalation, and the gentleman turned up at the TO staff and we agreed to issue a joint declaration that would be broadcast on the local radio station on the next morning, and that gentleman was full of understanding and agreement with Mr. Muhamedagic. We appealed to the people. That is he was the first one to do so, saying that all Muslims who had weapons, that they should refrain from any attacks in connection with the attack at Blagaj during the previous night. I, too, as the president of the Municipal Assembly appealed to all citizens of the municipality to refrain from any arbitrary action and we gave instructions saying that the legal bodies such as the TO and the public security station would do their utmost to preserve law and order. That is what happened during that night and what I know in connection with that attack. What kind of impact it had in the context of the armed attack of that night I cannot say. If you understand me correctly, then you would have understood that it was my task as president of the Municipal Assembly to try to act to -- in terms of general prevention over the radio. So both I and the SDA president, we are both persons in public office who tried to prevent escalation. However, there wasn't much effect, and the situation on the ground evolved more chaotically so that both ethnicities, both ethnic groups acted the way they thought proper. Both me and Mr. Muhamedagic were dissatisfied or at least I was with -- dissatisfied with what we had made public. And on the ground it was very different. There was shooting, there was refusal to disarm, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So the answer was no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you mean the order, if this is what you have in mind, the answer is yes -- or, rather, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So I take it that as a lawyer by profession, you should be able to answer succinctly. You may be offered why as to -- offered an opportunity to explain your position later on, but if you could concentrate on answering the question more succinctly. Do you understand that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you asked me whether I had issued that order, then the answer is no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given the time, we'll have a break for half an hour. Ms. Sutherland, you spent so far about an hour, so I take it you may be able to finish your cross-examination in an hour's time. But let us see how it --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The witness is giving extraordinarily long answers, at least 20 lines of transcript to practically every question. So I would respectfully ask if that could be taken into account.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll resume at 5 past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, if we can continue where we left off. If I could have 65 ter number 32814, please. Mr. Pasic, this is -- this is a Croatian intercept, and if we can -- I can draw your attention to the second paragraph of -- of the document that will come up on the screen. Here's what's reported up the 5th Corps chain of command on the 11th of May, 1992, by Major Zeljaja. Now, you know Major Zeljaja is from the neighbouring municipality of Prijedor, don't you? He was the deputy commander of the -- what was then the 343rd -- 334 -- 343rd Motorised Brigade in Prijedor. And this is what he says.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me. She's not giving him a chance to answer any questions. She asked him: You know this person and then she just kept going on. He needs to answer the question before she moves on to the next part of her question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Point taken.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, do you know Major Zeljaja?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: I heard of him. I may have seen him once or twice. I can't remember. I don't even know where I saw him. He was not in Novi Grad municipality, so his name doesn't mean that much to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay. This is what he's reporting up his chain of command: "At 1840 hours, Major Zeljaja informed Colonel Devic who forwarded the information to the general that the following event took place in Blagaj: According to the order of president of Bosanski Novi municipality, the Serbs opened fire at Muslim villages from artillery and mortars. That was not necessary because the measures had been already taken; everyone had been disarmed and everything had been 'ocisceno' 'mopped up or cleansed.' They are completely crazy extremists led by the municipality president." So this document here has the military being intercepted by the Croatian authorities and says that you ordered the attack on the village. You did issue orders to the TO to shell -- and others to shell Muslim villages; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: No. This is another leading question. I've already answered. I can repeat a hundred times. I didn't issue any order. I don't know where Mr. Zeljaja got this information from. I don't know that. And his use of their derogatory terms, that's up to him. In any case, things like that did not happen, and I adhere by what I previously stated.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd ask that this be marked for identification at this stage, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But you agree that you were the then president of Bosanski Novi municipality. Yes. We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6436 marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, in paragraphs 54 and 55 of your statement referring to adjudicated facts 2285 and 611, you -- you state that there was no shelling of these villages, there was no heavy artillery, and this is -- this is the Muslim villages in the Japra valley such as Hozici and Agici. You say that you think that shelling and arson didn't exist but -- but it could have been by unknown persons. You state that you think that it simply -- the village guards, Serbs in the Serbian villages and Muslims in the Muslim villages shooting at each other. We have a report which is from the chief of the SJB in Bosanski Novi, and that's part of Exhibit D00470 where he details events from April until August, and in that document at e-court page 17 in the English and page 22 in the B/C/S, he says that as a result of -- of this one incident with the military police patrol that as a result of that a series of combat operations were directed against areas and villages with a majority Muslim population, and then he goes on to say: All the combat operations mentioned above were carried out by armed uniformed mean who were either self-organised or members of the TO or JNA combat units. And in fact if I can just take you to some testimony which was given by Midho Alic in the Krajisnik case, and this is at transcript page 2518 to 2519 and 2520 to 2521, and he says there about seeing a tank surrounded by Serb soldiers people from reserve unit forces. And he was asked: Was the removal of people from your village -- did it appear to be organised or did it appear to be a random event carried out by paramilitary organisations? "It was" -- "A. It was organised. Everything was organised. First the entire Japra valley was pushed into Blagaj Japra and then everyone who found themselves in Blagaj Japra was moved on." And then as they were walking out he saw the houses and barns burning. Another gentleman BT 83 talks about the shelling on the 12th of May and this is at transcript pages 14055 to 58, the soldiers start moving towards the village and then as the shelling began, more and more people were coming in -- in vehicles and -- and cars or whatever. So it's a fact, isn't it, that -- that it wasn't organised by the -- by the TO forces and others and JNA combat units and it wasn't simply these paramilitaries as you speak of.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: You're asking me to answer your questions and I don't know anything about that, and you want me to provide a brief answer. First of all, you're presenting facts which are not correct, and I would have to provide a lengthy answer. I've already said that during that period of time the JNA no longer existed, so the JNA could not be involved in any operations there because it didn't exist. I told you what the role of the TO staff was and how it acted. You obviously did not understand what the role of the president of a Municipal Assembly was and what my role was. My role concerned the civilian part of the tasks, if I may put it that way, and the subordination along the command lines, along the military command lines did not exist nor could it exist. I was not in a position to issue orders or command certain operations as you are putting it to me. The witness that you mentioned, I really don't know who that is. I don't think that the municipality of Bosanski Novi is aware of him having discharged any duties and based on that being able to say something more relevant about those events. I don't know whether that was his personal perception. I don't know that. However, what you presented in your question I would like to say that I still adhere by the same things and that the term "shelling" has not been fully explained, and you are persisting and you are insisting on claiming that the TO staff had heavy artillery and that they opened fire on villages, and I adhere by the fact that the TO staff did not have heavy artillery, that they didn't open fire without any reason, and this is what I'm telling you from my knowledge. And there were places where resistance was being put up, and there was fire being opened from there, and they were the ones who were involved in certain activities. According to your question, you are trying to say that those people were completely helpless, that they had not been involved in any activities and that there was shelling against them, and that's what you mention. I didn't say that. I wasn't witness to that. In my view, that didn't happen. When the TO staff organised actions, and they did, but those were just attempts to disarm those paramilitary formations, and wherever there was resistance to those attempts reactions ensued.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So these --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Those were armed actions if we may call it that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So these paramilitary formations that you're talking about you're saying that they're Muslim formations and they were shelling themselves, were they?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: You did not understand me well. This is an ironic question. My answer was not ironic. You cannot present my thoughts in any way you want because this is not what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, I want to move on now to talk about civilian matters. In -- in -- it's your position now and always has been that the non-Serb population were leaving Bosanski Novi of their own free will. They voluntarily left; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes. If we're talking about the departure of Muslims which was organised at the request of Muslim representatives.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you say the only reason there were discussions about Muslims leaving was because you couldn't protect them; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, that was true. I already told you that we had a big problem, and when I said "we," I mean the institutions of local authorities. We had a big problem with paramilitary formations which also involved Serbs. Those were primarily groups that had illegally crossed the River Una which is in Croatia now and they were under nobody's control. They were not under the control of any civilian or military authorities in Novi Grad. They presented a huge problem to us. We didn't know how to establish public law and order. We felt insecurity. Everybody did. Not only Muslims, the Serbs as well felt insecurity. The war already waged in Bosnia-Herzegovina. People were dying on the front lines. People felt insecurity even in the depth of the territory where there were no military activities, and those were due to groups that were not under anybody's control. We could not put them under our control, and I've already told you why. One of the reasons was the fact that those people did not hail from our own municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, the fact is -- a big factor in suggesting these evacuations was the threat that the Muslims were supposedly posing to the Serbs; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look at Exhibit P9-- 2918, sorry. P2918. Mr. Pasic, you're familiar with this document you've seen it before. It's a document dated the 8th of June, and it's issued by the Bosanski Novi Crisis Staff, and it informs citizens of Blagaj and the Japra valley that the Crisis Staff is ready to enable them to move out in an organised column and basically if they refuse this offer the Crisis Staff is unable to ensure their safety. Now, we can see this is signed on your behalf. Can you make out the signature?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: It's rather illegible. I cannot --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: We actually have a --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: -- decipher the signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: We have a better copy here which can be passed to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Usher. If it can be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We have it here so we don't have to put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, it -- this -- this document, this doesn't seem to be like the Muslims are leaving voluntarily.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: You asked me about the signature. So let's take things at a time. I can't decipher the signature. I don't know who signed the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay. Do you --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: May I continue?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you call this voluntary?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Whatever I've already said and whatever I've stated is not contrary to this information. I don't see that anybody threatened or forced people to do what they didn't want to do. This is just a piece of information. And you see that the Crisis Staff is trying to portray the real situation, and they say that they cannot provide any absolute guarantees not only to the non-Serbians but to anybody. I believe that, and I assume that there was a greater fear among Muslims, but we could not provide them with any guarantees that their houses, property, and lives would be safe. In that sense this information was dispatched. I don't know who signed on my behalf, but that was the gist of the text. The representatives of the Muslims wanted to leave voluntarily. They -- they wanted to leave Novi Grad of their own will, and this is what we are constantly being blamed for. We are being blamed of trying to put pressure on them to leave in an organised manner. I still adhere by my previous claim, and that is that not for a single moment did legal authorities, and I mean the municipal bodies, the SJB, the TO staff, the Executive Council of the municipality, the Crisis Staff, not for a single moment there was a willingness among them to forcibly remove people from their own houses and from their own homes. But you have to understand that there was a whirlwind of war, and Bosanski Novi was not isolated. A climate of instability had been created, and nobody trusted anybody irrespective of the position they occupied. It was impossible to provide anybody with guarantees of safety and ask them to -- to stay. This is the sense of this information. It says here that for objective reasons we are not able to take that kind of risk upon ourselves. We cannot say -- we cannot tell anybody that they can go on living safely here. This is the gist of this message, and I am interpreting what you can read. So I suppose that those people were aware of the situation. They were aware of the overall situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that's why they wanted to withdraw, to move out, to resettle, call it what you will, from the area in order to wait for the end of the war and for an opportunity to come back home. This was the gist of this information where they really expressed the desire to temporarily leave the area and wait for the end of the war, and that's what we heard in conversations.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are several reasons and motives for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are please speak slowly and simply.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, in paragraph 58 you say that there's no motive, no desire, to intention to evict the population. In fact, that -- that's not true. There was a policy to remove the Muslim population. You -- at this time, this document's dated the 8th of -- of -- of June, but -- but the day before that, on the 7th of June, there was a meeting of representatives of seven municipalities in the Sana-Una region, and that's Exhibit P02641, and at that meeting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before moving off from this document. Mr. Pasic, do you agree that this is your document, whoever signed this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, now -- well, not my document. It says Crisis Staff up here, and it's probably somebody who signed this on behalf of the "Crisis Staff", so let's say yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I note that from the -- through the e-court it was admitted only for reference purpose and now we can admit it in full.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if Mr. Usher can get the original back from Mr. Pasic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic in this meeting in -- held in Sanski Most on the 7th of June, there was municipalities' representatives from Bihac, Bosanski Petrovac, Srpska Krupa, which I take to be Bosanska Krupa, Sanski Most, Prijedor, Bosanski Novi, and Kljuc. And these conclusions were sent to the Crisis Staff of the autonomous region Krajina, the leadership of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Sarajevo, and to the 1st Krajina Corps in Banja Luka. Now, the sixth demand at this meeting was that: "All seven municipalities in our subregion agree that Muslims and Croats should move out of our municipalities until a level is reached where Serbian authority can be maintained and implemented on its own territory in each of these municipalities." If we --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Was that a question?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- just pause there. We're having -- problem getting the document up. Now, do you recall attending this meeting on the 7th of June?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Well, I remember some meetings. Well, look, these were very tempestuous times. It's hard to tell which day it was. I know that sometimes I had meetings in Prijedor, Novi, Sanski Most, Banja Luka, but specifically on that day I cannot say with full certainty that I was there. Well, it's possible that I was there, but I don't know what you meant, what you're asking about. Actually, I don't find that very clear so I cannot say with certainty that I was in Sanski Most on that day. Also take into account all the time that's elapsed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
