utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the provenance of this document if we cannot see it?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can the document not be brought up in e-court? 2641, P2641. Now, if we can go to the second page.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: We can see the sixth point -- bullet point, and we can also see a stamp at the bottom. I think it says SDS Municipal Board in Sanski Most. Now, do you recall being at this meeting where this -- sorry, you said that you attended many meetings in Prijedor and Sanski Most, but with this particular aspect, did you attend meetings where this issue was discussed about moving people out?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Well, I've already said that I cannot recall the exact date when I was in Sanski Most, and at other meetings, of course, but I do know that meetings were held in relation to war developments and the possibility of resolving problems related to supplies, electricity, fuel, crude oil, petrol. All communications were cut off, both facing Serbia and Croatia. So there was a series of problems, and this escalated --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. -- Mr. --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: I mean, there were such discussions but --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You remember going to meetings and you remember talking about supplies and electricity and fuel, but you don't recall meetings where they were discussing moving out the territory to an acceptable level? Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Well, you're either getting misinterpretations or you and I simply do not understand each other. I'm not trying to avoid your questions in any way, but you have to put them in a specific manner. I am telling you about the things I remember. I know that at such meetings there were discussions, and I was specifically talking about the municipality I came from. There was this willingness, so part of the Muslim population, not everybody, wanted to leave the territory of then Bosanski Novi temporarily.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. -- Mr. Pasic, sorry --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: However, I was not saying that that was the only discussion that took place.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: We're just seeing the beginning of this paragraph and it says: All seven municipalities in our subregion, of which Bosanski Novi is one, agree that Muslims and Croats should move out of our municipalities until a level is reached. My question is: Is it your evidence that you do not -- you do not recall attending meetings where this was discussed and you -- and -- and -- and if the answer is no to that, that you weren't briefed by whoever the representative from Bosanski Novi was on such an important issue as moving the population out of your municipality of which you're the president of?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, may I make a suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Can he answer the first question first before we go to the second one?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, I think I've asked you a couple of times now. Is it your -- is it your position that you don't recall attending any meetings, whether it's on the 7th of June or the 14th of June, where these sorts of issues were discussed? Now, you can remember attending meetings about electricity and so forth, but is it your evidence that you don't recall attending meetings to discuss -- that discuss this issue?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: You interrupt me very often and I cannot give adequate answers to certain questions. It's as if you were trying to confuse me, but that's not the issue. You are not going to confuse me. I want to provide the truth, and I want to provide accurate information. So all of this works to your detriment, not mine, because you're the one who's interrupting me. I said that I attended numerous meetings and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. No. It is for the Prosecution to ask you questions. It's for you to answer the question. You have before you a document which is called "Conclusion," which we have admitted into our evidence. She read out a certain passage in point 6, and the question was whether you remember -- you remember having attended a meeting where such issue was discussed. Your answer could be no or yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not remember these things, that it was only this that was discussed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So the second question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't understand you, "I do not remember these things, that it was only this that was discussed." So you remember having attended meetings where this kind of issue was a part of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you cannot understand when you're just asking me to give a yes or no answer. It's impossible to answer that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then it's your problem. Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I understood Mr. Pasic as saying that only electricity and fuel and supplies were -- were discussed. He --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Is that correct, Mr. Pasic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: That's not correct. I've been trying to be of assistance here, to say how things happened, but with these frequent interruptions you cannot give -- you cannot get the right information from me, and you either don't want to listen to me or you cannot just give yes or no answers. It was not that there was just one item on the agenda at a single meeting and it was not only one thing that was discussed at a meeting. And I who attended these meetings, I did not review the conclusions how somebody formulated this. Somebody could present this in a different way, get the wording wrong without me knowing about it. At these meetings as I've already said it wasn't that it was only electricity, water, telephones that were discussed, but also the problem of part of -- well, everybody presented their own problems. Specifically I at these meetings presented the problem that had to do with the municipality of Novi Grad. I presented the problem that part of the Muslim population from the territory of the municipality of Bosanski Novi wanted to go to third countries in Western Europe and also that we had certain discussions with representatives of the UN where they categorically refused that from the very outset and it was the representatives of the Muslims that insisted on this. So these were the discussions that were held. These are conclusion -- the conclusions that I have. I cannot remember that, but it's very hard to just give a yes or no answer, because this is not the only information that can be provided and you cannot get the right idea what was happening at these meetings and how certain conclusions were made. If you want to get the right kind of information then these things have to be talked about a lot more extensively. As for the environment that we were at the time, there was a series of circumstances that affected everything, and also this text itself. I mean, I almost never saw the form in which it was written. Perhaps somebody wrote something like that in such strong language out of ignorance, and now that is being abused. But I still stand by the fact that you unfortunately do not believe because you keep saying that we wanted to expel the Muslims. That was not the objective of the Crisis Staff or of my own or of the authorities of Novi Grad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably the question was not precisely formulated. Do you remember having attended a meeting where a conclusion reached to the effect that Muslims and Croats should move out of your municipalities until a level is reached where Serbian authority can be maintained and implemented on its own territory in each of these municipalities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recall being advised by anyone else from the Bosanski Novi municipality of this?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: You mean meetings like this where this was --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, this specific issue. Do you ever -- do you recall being briefed by someone else from Bosanski Novi that this issue had been discussed?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Well, look, quite simply even if we had that wish, there was no need for that, and there was no need for us to talk about this or think about this. The Crisis Staff did not need to think about this for a simple reason: Muslims were initiating their open departure. That is to say their representatives were asking for that. So what you've been asking me about, there was simply no need for that because the representatives of the Muslim people were seeking ways and means of moving out of the municipality of Novi Grad. Quite simply this question could not have been brought up as such because there was not that kind of environment for us to be thinking about that; that is to say we did not have any need to think about that. For us to force someone to leave that would have meant that somebody was resisting that. You keep saying persecution, that these people were driven out. No. These people just asked us as representatives of the authorities to help us find the most adequate, painless, and best solutions to leave this area. There was no need for that kind of thing, and it did not -- it was not supposed to exist in the first place, and I don't know whether you understand me and what you were trying to say in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we can just go to page 1 of this document. Mr. Pasic, you'll see that demand number 4 -- well, conclusion number 4 of this subregional meeting which included Bosanski Novi, you demand that the 1st Krajina Corps in Banja Luka, particularly General Momir Talic of the 1st Krajina Corps purged the 1 KK of Muslims and Croatia. Now, do you remember being at a meeting when that was discussed?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: I remember this question because you insist on it so much. I think that someone allegedly stated that, I think from the government of the ARK Krajina. I really do not recall this context, that it existed that way. I think that this is formulated in the wrong way. This is my personal position. What was meant was that there were certain people, by now it was already the Army of Republika Srpska. There were certain people of other ethnicities worked along parallel lines for the VRS and also for the army of the Muslims. What was it called, the so-called Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time. So I think from that point of view attention was supposed to be paid to this kind of thing, espionage, treason if we can call it that. I'm not saying that this is my personal position. I mean, I'm not saying that it's the way it is written here, but during my earlier testimony when I looked at these documents, again I'm saying that this is my subjective observation. I'm not making any assertions here, but also I cannot refute the story that we read here. However, I repeat once again that at these meetings my only problem was the situation on the ground in the municipality of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In principle I'm not saying that I wasn't interested in how things were in other municipalities, but I was not competent to decide on the situation in Sanski Most, Kljuc, Banja Luka, any other municipality. That was not within my own purview. I could simply take note of that and --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've avoided interrupting the witness up until now but he's being unresponsive to the -- to the question and getting far away from -- from what I was asking him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we have a 65 ter number 05758 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, this is a command of the 1st Krajina Corps report on the ARK Crisis Staff decision submitted to the Serbian Republic of BiH Army Main Staff and to the Serbian Republic BH Presidency, and it states that one of the issues that was discussed at yesterday's session of the ARK Crisis Staff was the general -- there's no policy in the army of the 1st Krajina Corps, and it states that an ultimatum was issued requesting the removal of 67 officers of Muslim and Croat nationality. And then it states that the 1st Krajina Corps consider that the demand to be justified. So it appears, does it not, that these people, for the reasons that were discussed at the 7th of June, 1992, meeting, were not going to be permitted to return once they were removed.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: What's the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The question is: This -- this document -- so we start with the 7th of June conclusions at the -- of the seven municipalities. They then demand from the 1st Krajina Corps to purge the 1 KK of the Muslims and the Croats and then we can see this document here where the 1 KK are saying that the issue was discussed at yesterday's ARK Crisis Staff meeting and now they're saying that they have to make a decision about the 67 officers -- are members in the army. So I'm saying that this was followed up from this earlier conclusion it appears, does it not?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: You keep expecting me to answer questions about something that I do not know about and cannot know about. Let's say that these documents are accurate, but somebody else wrote that, and you'd really have to ask those people, those services that wrote this what their motive and intentions were. I could not have known what people were writing about from the command of the 1st Corps and who they were writing to. This was absolutely not within my authority. And from this you draw the conclusion seven municipalities. Whether somebody signed this, wrote this, this is a series of questions that you are putting to me, and you're asking me to give short and precise answers. That is absolutely impossible. I want to talk about the things I know here, things that I had at my disposal and that I remember. If you're asking me to give answers about this I really cannot because I simply don't know about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Pasic, I'll take you to -- to a document where it appears that you were present at, and that is 65 ter 25344, please. Now, Mr. Pasic, this is -- this is a document related to this second inter-municipality talks held in Korcanica on the 14th of June, 1992. And we can see that you are listed at number 11. You were shown a copy of this document in the Krajisnik trial and you said that it was your handwriting and you didn't recall attending this meeting. And that was at transcript page 17980. You said that you had been to meetings between the municipalities and you said that earlier today in your evidence, and in that document it states that most of the 7 June 1992 suggestions have been accepted which includes the purging of the Muslims and Croats from the army and in relation to getting the population down they were -- until the demands included in the 7th of June conclusions? So --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Could you tell us where you're reading from in that document?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The first paragraph, "As far as the previous meeting" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do we have it?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry. If we can turn to the next page. My mistake.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: "As far as the previous meeting of the Autonomous Region of Krajina Crisis Staff is concerned, we can conclude that most of our suggestions have been accepted and became part of the official position of the Crisis Staff at a meeting held on the 8th of June, 1992. We demand a decisive and clear response to each conclusion made then and the personal responsibility of those who were in charge of implementing each conclusion." So does this refresh your memory about those two issues?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Well, I find this question familiar because it was heard during my previous testimony, and I have nothing to add to what I stated then. I absolutely do not remember this meeting at Korcanica, and it's correct what you showed me earlier on, that that is my name and surname and that is my signature. However, I really do not recall these things, and I think that this is a forgery. Somebody scanned my signature and then attached it to this document. I have to highlight one particular matter if you allow me to do so, of course. Very often some people at some meetings -- well, what was addressed to the military command, the 1st Krajina Corps, and so on. Perhaps sometimes attempts were made to create more seriousness because say the civilian authorities thought that they were not doing things on time in order to create public law and order. Now, whether something like that was written here and which is wrong and which was not discussed at certain meetings. Well, I'm not going to say that that is the case, but I'm not going to confirm or deny this. I really don't know. Just like then I did not remember, and I don't remember now either that I attended this kind of meeting at Korcanica. I know that I was at Korcanica only once in my life. This is on Mount Grmic which is a mountain. Perhaps I would have attended that meeting, but I assume that in this period -- it says here the 14th of July. That period was so difficult and shaky and the municipality of Bosanski Novi that I had - how do I put this? - far greater problems in resolving vital issues and I did not attend that meeting probably because of that because subjectively I could not have been there not for any other reasons. So I'm not trying to avoid your question or, rather, answering your question, but I simply cannot confirm that I attended this meeting because I remember no such thing and I do not remember these positions that were addressed to the 1st Krajina Corps, at least it seems to me that that is what it written here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender that document from the command of the 1 KK.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. First of all, I assume she's now speaking of a document we looked at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's find out what document she's tendering first.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: 05758, the one dated the 9th of June, 1992, the one that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Not this one?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Oh, sorry, no. I want to tender both documents. Yes, because this is -- this is a 65 ter number as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any objection to the admission of this document, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I don't believe that the witness -- he said he didn't know anything about it, doesn't recall attending the meeting and it might be a forgery. So I think with that -- kind of answers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But the witness confirmed that this looked like his sit. It may be -- it might have been scanned, but at first he admitted his signature, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, if that -- if that's the basis upon which you think you have enough reliability to admit this then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me ask Mr. Pasic again. Do you agree that the signature you saw was yours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I said that. This is my signature. But whether it was on this document then in this form, I don't know. I'm not denying that this is my signature, but I'm not sure that this is the meeting in question or that -- or that this -- this signature of mine was put on this list of names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit this one.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6437, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And can I hear your submission about 5758, if Ms. Sutherland is tendering that document as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Also if I would just remind Ms. Sutherland it's a lot better to tender these documents at the time they're offered or the time they're discussed. But going back to pages 55 and 56 of the transcript, the witness said he didn't know anything about this, so there's no basis to admit it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, the reason why I didn't seek to tender it when it was used was because I wanted to bring this document up to show that it makes mention of the out-Crisis Staff meeting held on the 8th of June which is referred to in the 9th of June document that I showed. And so that's why I didn't do it at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure ...

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, we can see from this document that's on the screen, the 14th of June document, where the cover page has Mr. Pasic attending. He disputes that fact. It goes -- it's -- it's a matter of weight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Although 5758 was dated as 9th of June --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- the meeting itself --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It refers to a meeting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- was held on the 8th of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, and of course that meeting of the 8th of June of the out-Crisis Staff is referred to in paragraph 1 of this document that we have on the screen. 65 ter -- the one that you've just admitted, 25344.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you upload 5758 for a short moment, English as well, yes. Thank you. Where does it say that this meeting was held on the 8th?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It says one of the issues that was discussed at yesterday's meeting of the ARK Crisis Staff, and the document is dated the 9th of June. So it makes sense that it's a meeting held by the ARK Crisis Staff on the 8th of June, which is the meeting that's referred to in the 14th of June document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But this document itself was not referred to in -- in the inter-municipality agreement was it?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No. On the 7th of June the two things that I drew Mr. Pasic's attention to: One was the moving out of the population, that was demand number 6; and then the other one was demand number 4, about purging Muslims and Croats from the army. That's on the 7th. It's then discussed at the ARK Crisis Staff on the 8th. Then this document is -- is on the 9th from the -- the -- the 1st Krajina Corps to the Main Staff, and then there's a Main Staff exhibit which I'm not going to bring up, an order signed by General Mladic on the 9th, and that's Exhibit P05469 which states that the Muslim Croat nationality must be sent on leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to add anything, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just one broad point since the Court raised the question. I -- I -- if I understood the Court's question correctly whether or not this specific document was referenced in the other document would seem to go to authentication, which is a matter not at issue here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. The witness said he didn't know anything about this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, no, but the -- the issue. That's why I raised the authentication versus subject matter issue. The subject matter however is very much at issue and therefore very much goes to credibility and to impeachment which is one of the factors, of course, we've used consistently for admission of such documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber is of the view that document may be related to the credibility of this witness. On that basis, we'll admit that as well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6438, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And just for the record I wasn't clear when I was saying it goes to the weight of it. That was exactly what I meant and I should have been clearer that I said when you're weighing up his credibility, then -- but -- Your Honour, I think my time is -- is up, but given the extraordinarily long answers that the witness has given to nearly every question, there's one or topic that I wish to deal with and I think I can do it in 15 or 20 minutes at most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, you have referred earlier in your evidence today about your -- you were involved in negotiations with the UN and other Muslim representatives -- sorry, other representatives of all the Muslims in Bosanski Novi about them moving out, and you talk in paragraph 59 about meetings in Dvor, the UN -- the UNPROFOR base, meetings in Topusko, meetings on the bridge of the River Una. And in paragraph 20 of your statement you mention that representatives of the Muslim community asked to leave peacefully from the area and that they wanted to leave of their own free will, and you mentioned three people as being the most prominent.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I would ask that we go into private session momentarily.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Pasic, Mr. Nemin Puric --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: No, that's not the right name. Can I help you?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I think you may -- are you going to say his name's Emin Puric?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Well, if you let me, I will tell you the name. May I?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: The people in question are of Muslim ethnicity, and they attended the meetings. One of them is Emin Puric, the other is Amin Delic, then there was Senad Brkic and Nedim Muftic, and some others whom I don't remember now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, you're correct. I've just been advised it's Emin Puric, not Nemin Puric. Anyway, he -- he says when he's -- when he's asked about you he said: Well, we knew each other very well. And this is at transcript page 26993 to 26994. We worked together. I knew -- I know his character. At the time he seemed to be a changed person. He talked in a very authoritarian manner. And then down a few lines he says: I remember that well. He said, referring to you, "No, they cannot stay here." And you could sense that the whole atmosphere was that they wanted us to go, to leave, which suited us as well, I must admit, because if it had not been for that will it would have been difficult for us to get organised and to leave that chaos behind. And at page 26998 to 27000, when the Judge said: You used rather strong words when you said that you all wanted to leave, could you tell us because until now I see that people were -- houses were search. They were taken to a school. They had to stay there for two days and were allowed to return home. Could you perhaps first indicate briefly what the kinds of events were that made you decide that the situation was too bad to stay? And he answered: Well, you know what? When 10.000 people believe that it is their lucky day, when they are leaving their homes and everything, then I had to consider myself to be very -- I had to consider myself to be lucky too to leave that hell. At transcript page 27007 to 27009 the Presiding Judge asks him again: When you had these meetings, as you said, two meetings on the bridge, first of all, were you aware of any people staying at that moment, if it was at that moment, in the Mlakve stadium? And he said, Yes I knew that and I said something about that the first time I went to Dvor, to the UNPROFOR staff. They said that they knew about the existence of that, that they were monitoring and observing that location. We knew about that the whole time. And if I may add, when we were talking with these representatives, I mean with Mr. Pasic, we asked, I did and the people that you see here, we said that we would not leave unless the people from the stadium were released as well. We did not want to leave unless all the people were released from the stadium as well, and they said that they would be released. And at 27009 to 27013, the Presiding Judge asks him to comment on paramilitaries out of control being blamed for what happened, and he says, When Mr. Jens asked that the authorities impose order and improve the security situation and prevent those who were committing these murders and so Mr. Drazic said that was not done by the regulars of the Territorial Defence -- by the regulars or the Territorial Defence, as he said, but this was done by groups who had -- who were no longer under anyone's control. I said that this was not true and that this could very easily be resolved if there was goodwill to do that. Then Mr. Jensen said, "How could this be done?" I said: We could deal with this very simply if we were to set up mixed or joint guards because at that time you had different guard duties on the entrance to villages, junctions and so on, but they were exclusively Serb people in those guards and I just said, well, let's make mixed or joint guards and then they would receive weapons and then each side could deal with their own people -- if she could come up and this could be done very easily. However, Mr. Drazic said that this could not be done, that this cannot be prevented. These groups were out of control and it wasn't possible to do anything about that, but I think that that wasn't true. The Crisis Staff knew who was doing that. They knew everything by name. They knew about people being taken away, people getting killed, and so forth. And then a few lines down the Presiding Judge says: One more question about the negotiations on the bridge. You asked permission to leave and I do understand that it was more than fully supported that it was even required that you should leave. Did you ever raise the issue of returning to your own places, the places where you lived? Was that ever a subject discussed during these negotiations? And he answered: You mean negotiations before we left in the convoy? The Judge said: Yes, that's what I meant. He answered: No. It was pointless to even mention this to them. It was a question that had no sense at all at that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I have to interrupt, Ms. Sutherland. You are entering the fourth page of the transcript in one question. I'm not sure how the witness can answer your question if your question is so lengthy.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I want to put these excerpts to him and then to put a question to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think that's an efficient way, but could you break it down. Let's give it a try. Let's ask him a question now and let's see whether he's able to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, the excerpts that I've just read to you so far from -- from the -- the witness's testimony, that -- that's not of a person who is wanting to leave his home where he's lived for generations, is it? He's not leaving voluntarily. He's leaving because he's being forced to leave by what the authorities have done or aren't doing.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Well, to such a long question I hope I'll be allowed to answer in two or three questions. I don't know what Emin Puric said here by way of testifying and what made him change the faithful image of the situation at the time when the negotiations were in progress. I know that you don't believe much what I'm saying here, but I do recommend to look at a video-clip that exists and listen to what Mr. Jensen said. I don't think he ever testified here. He negotiated on the bridge. He also doubted that -- or, rather, he had his suspicions that people were leaving because of threats. I'm not sure of his name, Jensen or Jens, but there is his picture available. I can show it to you. And without my knowledge and without the knowledge of the local authorities, he went to a Muslim family and spoke to them clandestinely. We -- they tried to prevent a set-up, because we might send them to some of our own Muslims, in inverted commas, so he had the opportunity to talk to some Muslims and see what the situation was really like and find out whether they were leaving voluntarily or they were being driven out. Mr. Jensen did that or, rather, his delegation, and I still don't know which families those were and which people and when exactly it was. It was some time in June or July when he had these conversations and that may have been the decisive factor for the decision of the UNHCR in Topusko, and what their -- what was the motivation of the Muslims to leave. It was a decision they took of their own free will. It wasn't due to our attitude or our desire to resolve the issue of Muslims in the Bosanski Novi municipality in this manner. There are video-clips where Mr. Puric insisted at that time that they were leaving of their own free will. I don't know whether this is -- this can be shown for the Trial Chamber. If it is in the interest of justice, and I'm sure that you want to learn the truth, but these facts are constantly misrepresented as someone's desire to drive out the Muslims from the Bosanski Novi municipality. It certainly wasn't the municipal authorities. Nobody was in the position to know about this from the top echelons of the RS because all the communications lines were down. Not even telex communication was possible. So the higher bodies didn't know about the situation. So it was our own plight, and it was up to our resourcefulness how we can overcome these local problems and resolve them. The Muslim population felt the need, in a way, to, conditionally speaking, find a safe haven with the United Nations at Topusko and that situation, my role and that of Mr. Drazic was a personal friend of Mr. Puric, and I also know Puric and he confirmed that. We weren't on bad terms and I have nothing against him personally. It was merely our attitude to assist them, to do as they wanted at the time, and why Mr. Puric said that or changed his mind due to pressures or whatever is something that he can tell you. This matter which to my mind is extremely important -- can you hear me? I really want to say that these people that were involved in us were saying very different things from what I have just been read out. They wanted to reunite their families who were in third countries and our region. They were guest workers who worked in Austria or Germany. They thought that the war would soon be over and that everybody would be all right. And that was the -- their opinion. So that it isn't true what Mr. Puric stated in his evidence. He must have been under some certain pressure. I never insisted that they go, but I spoke to Mr. Jensen and to Mr. Jean-Claude Konkolato [phoen] I think that was his name, and this gentleman also said some untruths when I spoke about Serbian refugees, and I asked the UNHCR to help everybody irrespective of their ethnicity, but he presented that as our wish, the wish of the municipal authorities to put up Serbs in Muslim houses. And I can say that there has never been such a thing. But it was our concern how Serbs who fled from Croatia should be assisted by the UNHCR to return to their homes or that their property status should be resolved somehow. Likewise we wanted to assist the Muslims in doing what they wanted. And this was a crucial issue. We may have been able to resolve all dilemmas if the -- Mr. Muhamedagic, the SDA leader, were alive. I'm very sorry that he died. And he personally in talking to me, and I don't remember the exact date, it was certainly after the start of combat operations, he told me that for a number of reasons they had decided, perhaps due to a feeling of military impotence, but they certainly decided to leave the area and that this was their initiative. And therefore I see no reason why it is -- why these persistent attempts to put the blame on the municipal authorities of Bosanski Novi because you're trying to say that we wanted to force them to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What Ms. Sutherland read out is not in our evidence, so the question was whether he was leaving voluntarily, and your answer was no; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They left voluntarily, so the answer is yes, they left of their own will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Let's continue, Ms. Sutherland. Do you have more questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Just -- just one follow-up, Mr. Pasic. You said that you never insisted that they go, but one of the men called by the Court in the Krajisnik case -- based on what you said he said that -- that you insisted, and secondly that armed soldiers, and this is -- this is Amin Delic now, I'll read what he said. He said: Armed soldiers started going door-to-door forcing them to leave, and this is transcript page 26358. Judge Orie is then -- then the Presiding Judge says: Talking about Mr. Pasic, during these negotiations did he show any awareness of the reasons why you wished to leave or did you tell him during these negotiations what urged you leave the territory of the municipality. And

utterances.speaker: MR. DELIC ANSWERED
utterances.text: Of course he was aware of it. He was the president of that Crisis Staff of the Bosanski Novi municipality, and he managed the whole thing. He supervised and controlled the situation in full. Mr. Pasic certainly had the situation under his complete control and he could have -- of course was aware of what was going on in town and what was happening to the people. During these negotiations he said that we had to leave and that we may not remain, and even -- and that even if we did remain, because the UNHCR representatives were telling us to stay, that they would bring us humanitarian aid --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Mr. Pasic, could you excuse yourself for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, this witness is saying that the Muslims or those Muslims left voluntarily. And you are confronting the witnesses -- witness with some other witness's testimony from other case. Am I correct in so understanding?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How does it affect the credibility of the witness when we -- such evidence is not in our proceedings?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, it -- what these two witnesses, the Court witnesses in the Krajisnik case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: They are not our witnesses and that transcript is not in evidence in our case.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: But it -- but it completely contradicts what he is saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How do we know which is correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm not -- I'm not sure that the Court was following the chronology here entirely which certainly makes this a different matter than impeachment by witness testimony. In this case this witness testified before this institution before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This witness, in order to vouch for his own credibility said, Go talk to these people. They'll back me up. The Court actually in a fairly rare and impressive moment followed up on that, called those people and this is what they said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. His evidence in the previous case was not admitted in our case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No. But I think he's -- I think he's acknowledged that he gave evidence there and that he did -- I think he confirmed that in fact he tried to vouch for his credibility before this institution in another case by citing these particular individuals, and that in fact the Court called his bluff and called those people and this is what they said.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, he refers to -- to these people in paragraph 20 of his statement before this Court in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That was the point I was asking. Paragraph 20. Did you have something to tell us, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I don't see anything wrong with the Prosecution confronting a witness with what another person has said about a relevant subject matter whether that was in testimony before this Court, a prior statement, a letter, a video, whatever, and then they have to take the witness's answer. What they're quoting is not evidence, and if the witness says, No, it was never my understanding that there was -- they didn't want to leave. That's the only evidence that you have. What is being put to the witness is not evidence, only the witness's answer. So I don't see that what Ms. Sutherland did was wrong except that it -- when she has lengthy extracts like that it's better to paraphrase and put the point to the witness instead of quoting everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Points well taken. In particular, I thank Mr. Robinson's statement with which I agree. Shall we take a break? The witness can be informed of the break by our Registry. We'll take a break for 45 minutes and resume at 1.20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, just to finish off what Mr. Amin Delic was saying to the Krajisnik Court, and this is at transcript page 26366. He said: However, there was no question on our side whether we were going or not, whether we had to run or not and there was no doubt on their side because everything had been done so that we would have. Mr. Pasic, what he's referring to, is he not, everything that had been done so that we would have to leave, was all the documentation that the witnesses -- that the Muslims had to fill out before they -- before they could leave?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: At the moment when UN representatives said they would be working on that issue, due to some legal obligations we suggested that people who wanted to leave the territory voluntary, who wanted to leave Bosanski Novi and Novi Grad should make arrangements for their property, a sale contract, an exchange of property, a donation, there were such things. All that was done with a view to protecting our property in a painless way. I told you already about those groups, the paramilitary formations, people wanting to make a quick gain, and so on and so forth. We wanted to protect property, for example, people could exchange their property for property of a Serb in Croatia or they could sell their property. Whatever was done, we thought that that kind of property would be better protected from destruction or any kind of a misuse. There were such things, of course. However, I would like to point out that some of the people did not have such documents at all, but that was not an obstacle for those who wanted to leave together with the people who had those documents and obtained such documents. According to what I know, there were such people of Muslim ethnicity who left at that time and did not obtain any documents. So that was not a condition for somebody to be able to leave voluntarily or to stay. So that was not a condition. It was not something that would have prevented them from leaving. It was simply not a condition for departure.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, these -- these two witnesses, the excerpts of their testimony that I've read out to you completely contradict your position, don't they?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: There is something in our judiciary system which is facing somebody eye-to-eye. I would like to be faced with these people. I would like us to look each other in the eye, and then we would know who's telling the truth, who's not. I don't know what Mr. Delic and Mr. Puric, what they said and why they changed their statement about the events in 1992. I adhere by my statement when I say that those people, representatives of the Muslims, wanted to leave the area. Why they changed their position in their testimony I can only assume, but I'm not competent to be the judge of why they testified falsely when they appeared before the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, you say that we suggested that these people who wanted to leave voluntarily. You could make arrangements and stuff, but why did you then make them sign documents that they were moving on a permanent basis?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: They were not forced. They were not forced to sign any documents at all. Under the laws that prevailed at that time, somebody could change their place of residence either temporarily or permanently. It was regulated by the law. Therefore, people who were moving out or going somewhere temporarily are entitled to some entitlements and have some obligations. On the other hand, people who are moving out permanently, nobody can forbid them to return. Again, there are some obligations that arise from that. If somebody changes their place of residence temporarily under the prevalent law they stop being a military conscript. They could not be considered deserters or somebody who failed to meet their legal military obligation. So that was just one part of the legal formulation if that's what you have in mind. Whether somebody left temporarily or permanently they could still change that position in a month, two months, or a year, and they could still return to their original place of residence. All the paperwork, all the decisions that were made by the local authorities were made to make note of those who were leaving and how their property relations were resolved and dealt with. That was the only thing that existed, how to arrange things when some of the population was leaving the municipality. That was the only intention of the local authorities, and that's why those documents were produced and had to be obtained.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, I want to just --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... [overlapping speakers] transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that on line 4 the witness said that they stopped being military conscripts if they changed their place of residence permanently, whereas on line 4 it has been recorded that that happened that if they changed their place of residence temporarily. I don't know what the provisions of the law were. Maybe the witness could clarify. I believe that I heard the witness say that they -- when they changed their place of residence permanently they stopped being military conscripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Is that right, Mr. Pasic? You said -- you said the word "permanent" when you were referring to the change of residence when you spoke a moment ago? Please don't repeat your whole answer. Can you just say whether you agree what Mr. Karadzic just put to you.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Well, you asked me about those two categories, temporary and permanent. I can explain the meanings of the two terms, but maybe that will be too long. I can explain the meaning of the word "temporary" as opposed to the word "permanent."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. We're talking about the transcript, whether it precisely reflected your answer. So you can answer yes or no whether Mr. Karadzic said is correct or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood Mr. Karadzic perfectly, and I believe that what he said is absolutely correct. There is a difference between temporary residence and permanent residence. I don't know how the interpreters are going to interpret that, but my understanding of Mr. Karadzic's question is absolutely perfect.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be of assistance? When it comes to people being military conscripts, will they lose their status as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, that's a subject matter you can take up in your re-examination. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Can I have 65 ter number 08812.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, this is -- I want to -- you to have a look at this document. It's dated the 9th of July, 1992, and it's a document that Midho Alic had to sign in order to -- to move out. Is that the documentation that you were talking about a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: It's not very legible. Can this be zoomed in or perhaps you have a hard copy of the original for my perusal. Is there a hard copy? This is not legible. The copy's not legible, the one that I have on the clean. Do you have a hard copy?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We can collapse the English and magnify the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Show him the bottom part as well. Yes. Let us know when you're done with your reading.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm reading. I am not familiar with the text of the statement. I don't know whether that was the wording. I can see that there is a stamp. It's not legible, but I believe that it is credible. It is possible that there was such a wording of this statement but I repeat the term "temporary" as opposed to "temporary" [as interpreted] is treated completely different in our parts. However, I believe that this was to emphasise some other obligations that I have already mentioned. The category permanent may apply to some exceptions. I suppose that you have one thing in mind when you're showing me this. At that moment, this term could not have permanently prohibited anybody's return if they wanted to return. So this term "temporary" as opposed to "permanent" has a meaning only in terms of rights and obligations. It didn't have a political connotation meaning that somebody would be prohibited from returning to their home for political, religious, or other reason. That was never the intention. So this wording -- let's avoid any confusion. I'm just trying to confuse -- I'm trying to explain the meaning of the term "temporary" as opposed to the term "permanent" and why the wording was as I -- we can see it here. I believe that this statement is really correct and that it came from this administration in the municipality. I was physically unable to draft any texts or have them signed by people. There were services who did that. And somebody really used this formulation, this wording. I don't know why. It was not in the senses as you are trying to put it to me. It's not to mean that people would be forbidden from going back home for religious or some other reasons. It was for the reasons that I previously explained and those were, for example, legal or military reasons.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The -- the Trial Chamber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Give us a moment to assign a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6439, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber has heard evidence that the Muslims had to sign these documents that they were leaving in order -- to say that they were leaving voluntary, that they had to swear they were leaving permanently and that they could never go back to their homes, and I refer Your Honours to KDZ011 and that's Exhibit P03880. And, Mr. Pasic, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me. Was that a closing argument? I thought we were doing the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No. Mr. Pasic -- if he -- if he would like, he said earlier that the witness's -- that the Muslims were leaving voluntarily. I was putting to him that the Trial Chamber has evidence before it that the witnesses, before they were allowed to leave, had to sign that they were leaving voluntarily when, in fact, they had to say that they were -- they were leaving voluntarily and they were permanently leaving and signing over all their property.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, do you agree with -- that's the -- that's the evidence that's before this Trial Chamber, and you dispute that, do you?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: I dispute that, of course. I've already said that this statement was not a condition for somebody leaving or staying. I repeat, according to some other information, some of the people left without having signed this statement. That was -- this is not an argument for somebody's forcible departure or somebody's voluntary departure. There was no pressures put to bear by this type of document. Nobody had to state that they were leaving forever because they were forced to leave. This is simply not correct. This is a statement. This is not a contract. This is not a decision. This is not an order. This is a statement, a declaration made by a person who signed this before a body. It does not have a legal force, the force of a legal document, in the sense that based on this document that person would be forbidden to ever come back. I repeat, the categories of permanent and voluntarily departure, whatever you think of it, I'm saying that this is just one of the possible ways in which the local municipal authorities tried to set up some sort of records of those people who were staying and those people who wanted to leave the area, and that was the meaning of the statements. It provided us with a better insight into the people who decided to stay. It was wartime when you could not follow the movement of people and the situation as it was. There should have been paper trail of some people leaving, moving out in all sorts of ways. I have to point out that a lot of persons, a lot of individuals who had friends among Serbs crossed the border individually, and that's how they left. This is -- this was our message, a lesson that we learned. We thought that there should be a trace of those people who had left in one way or another. That's why we came up with these declarations or statements, because we wanted to know how those people left.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is speaking too fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. -- Mr. Pasic, the interpreters were not able to catch up with your speed. Probably -- but I think we have heard sufficiently. If necessary, Mr. Karadzic will take up further. Do you have any re-examination, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Excellency. I did not realise that Ms. Sutherland had finished her cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Pasic, while the document is on the screen, could you please read the first sentence under the name.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: It says here --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Where it says the -- the signatory, the person who took the minutes?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: This -- can this being zoomed in, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you read the first sentence in the preamble.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: The last word?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The first sentence.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: The first sentence where?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Before -- under the name Alic.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: That name is not on the screen, and that sentence is not on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I then read it? "The person concerned is appearing ..." can you see that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpret's note that we don't have the English translation on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What does it mean when the person was not invited?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Well, it means that a person came without having been summoned. They came of their own will. That's the interpretation of that word, the translation of that word.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Both of us have to speak slowly. We have to make breaks. It hasn't been recorded properly. After the name it says, "An uninvited person is appearing before the authority of his own free will." Now we can see it. In the English translation it is somewhat different. It says "of his own free will." I believe that it should be "uninvited" or perhaps something else would be better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when people change their place of permanent residence, what changes? Does one's status as a military conscript change and other things?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Of course. Persons who leave the territory for various reasons, on that occasion each and every citizen, and I hope this is the case in some other countries, too, they are supposed to meet certain obligations or exercise certain rights. They are supposed to meet some of the obligations that they had previously in order to be able to leave that place of residence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just slow down, please. And what about temporary residence? Does one still have the same obligations?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Well, look, as far as temporary residence is concerned, temporary departures, that was usually considered to be for a very short period of time. So this is a terminological obligation on the basis of the law. Somebody may be away for 5, 10, 15, or 20 days, or a bit longer than that but then they would return shortly. In that situation, such a person was not duty-bound to meet these obligations, if you will, because it was believed that that person would come back and meet all these obligations upon their return. That would be the difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Could you tell us whether the municipality is responsible for any damage done to immovable property or destruction of property? Would citizens sue the municipality if something happened to their property? Please keep it as short as possible. Did they have the right to sue, and would they sue if something happened to their immovable property?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: That's happening right now. The motto is "war damages." Citizens of Republika Srpska, Bosnia-Herzegovina have the right to compensation if their property had been damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If a person states that they do not have immovable property, can they then sue the municipality?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Well, it would be logical that persons cannot ask for something if that something does not exist in the first place. So in a way this leaves a trace, how people are leaving their property and on what conditions and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we take a look at P2918 briefly, please. Could we have the English version, too, please, because it's more legible. Please, Mr. Pasic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it Ms. Sutherland has a hard copy of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. We do have the hard copy of the original [microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Ms. Sutherland, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we have page 2 in English, because I'm not sure that this is identical, the two documents, I mean. I'm going to read this out in English, and can you explain this to us and it will be interpreted to you: [In English] "Departures through Croatia and Slovenia, organised by UNPROFOR, was attempted before without success. The passage towards Banja Luka remains free." [Interpretation] Was there this possibility for them to go to Banja Luka, and did they accept that or refuse that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: I think that in the statement provided in writing I explained that, but I shall repeat. In talks with representatives of the Muslim people, there were such things that were being mentioned, namely due to certain reasons, their reasons, not to go into all of that now, they would mention places where it was not that dangerous in terms of potential danger or real danger, and, for example, in area of Banja Luka, that is somewhere in the interior, and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please do slow down. The transcript needs to keep up.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: I shall repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Try to keep it short. You don't need so many words.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Specifically, there were many talks and offers were made to the representatives of the Muslim people to withdraw into the interior of Republika Srpska where it was calmer, or if they wished, they could go to an area that was under the control of the Bosnian Muslims, that is to say in the direction of Central Bosnia. In principle, they did not accept that, or if they did accept it, they did so unwillingly, but their exclusive goal was to go to the European Union, European countries, for several reasons, and I can mention all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D27009, could we please have that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we move out from this document, Mr. Pasic, in answer to the question of Ms. Sutherland related to this document, you said at one point in time the Crisis Staff didn't need this kind of a policy - I don't remember exact word - because Muslims initiated their departure voluntarily. Do you remember having said so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Roughly. I understand the content, the point of your question. I think I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you read out the last sentence of this document aloud.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And which document is this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You have the Serbian version on the left-hand side, on your screen.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: I think that it can be read more easily here. I have it here: "If these proposals are rejected, the Crisis Staff will no longer be able to guarantee the security of Muslims in this area." Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. To many people it must have sounded like a threat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, yes. That's the question for you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the way it was: Very often the Crisis Staff was asked to do something that was virtually impossible and something that they were not even charge of. Very often the Crisis Staff had to disassociate itself from certain things in this way. Very often we were asked to provide guarantees that in a certain area, certain location part of the population will live safely and that no one would maltreat them for any reason or attack them or whatever. So in that context, since that is what we were being asked for and that was not within the realm of the possible for us, and sometimes also in writing we wanted to make it known that we quite simply could not provide such guarantees to anyone. This guarantee could not exist, absolutely, not for the Serb population, not for the Muslim population. So the Crisis Staff did not have that power, did not have the jurisdiction, did not have the strength to guarantee anyone's security. That is why it was written so harshly perhaps, this sentence, but in no way, in no context -- I mean, if somebody thinks that it's written in a two-sided way, it's not that somebody is being told to leave the area. We just wanted -- well, unfortunately there was this picture that was not a happy one for anyone, but the wish was to present in very picturesque terms the situation that we all found ourselves in in that area. Perhaps that is the point of these texts that were written in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, can you remind us of where after these unsuccessful transports through Croatia, Slovenia, these citizens were, these citizens for whom the Crisis Staff cannot provide guarantees? Where were they and under what conditions?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: You mean before they left?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At the moment when they returned from these unsuccessful attempts a few days before that, when this information is being written where were they? Where were they put up? Were they at home or where were they?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Thank you for asking. If I can put it this way, there was an unsuccessful attempt. Please don't misinterpret this. This was for technical reasons. That was ten days before this departure. There was this column had been established when the non-Serb population took their own cars, buses, trucks, as organised by UNPROFOR, the High Commissioner for Refugees, they tried to go to Kostunica, Dubica, so that they could cross into Croatia at the point in Jasenovica. For technical reasons this failed, please let us not misinterpret this. The Croatian authorities did not allow that to happen. That took seven or eight hours in the afternoon. So these people who had all packed their things and wanted to leave, sometimes around -- at some point around midnight they returned home, and they were all at home until they went again to these third countries. So they were at their own homes. So during that period of time to the best of our ability we, the organs of authority, protected them. They were at their homes, and again after about ten days they left their homes. I think it was the 22nd or 23rd of July, and they went in the direction of Karlovac or, rather, Croatia, and that's where they crossed the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So they stayed for a month and a half after that first attempt?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: No, a bit less. I think it was a bit less than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please pause, and please utter the smallest number of words possible as slowly as possible. What was your position, the position of the authorities, towards people being moved out and using illegal means, unlawful means, as far as movement was concerned?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: If you're referring to the local government, we have things that have been left in writing. It is explicitly stated that all forms of force, threat, or anything like that was strictly prohibited.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D27009, could we have that now, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. That's -- in fact a different version of that is Exhibit D01916 already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this document is? I beg your pardon. The previous document, does it say in that better version whether somebody signed that on behalf of Radomir Pasic, because in the version that we had we could not see that and you can see that it is somebody signing for, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: I cannot see the signature here. It is very illegible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: I really cannot see the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please focus on the screen now and could you tell us about these conclusions that were reached by the municipality? It is the municipality and not the Crisis Staff. Can you tell us what this is?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: I cannot see the preamble up there so I cannot say whether it's the Crisis Staff or the municipality. However, it does seem to me, well, I cannot say with certainty, that the Municipal Assembly was in session during this period of time, and they were analysing the conclusions of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Please remove the English version and zoom in, and can you confirm whether this is a session of the Municipal Assembly that is being held on the 16th of June? Please look at the preamble.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes. It says up there the Assembly of Bosanski Novi, held on the 16th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 2, the second and third bullet points.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: You want me to read that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. The second and third bullet points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I do it now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Can we zoom out for the moment. I'm not sure whether the document you referred to is the exactly identical one.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] No, Your Honour, I said --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I said a different version of it is D01916.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Should we try it? Which seems to be more legible? Exhibit D1916. I think we can see your signature.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I'm going to ask for the other one to be admitted too because it was published will the Official Gazette of Bosanski Brod.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, yes, Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No problem, but for the sake of reading, shall we deal with this, if the content is identical, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I think it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So paragraph 2, and the second and third bullet points.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I would just like to ask for it to be enlarged. It was better the last time. May I read now. So I'm reading paragraph 2, bullet point 1: "The citizens of Muslim ethnicity --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We have it here in English as well. You read it yourself, and then let us know when you are done reading. Then Mr. Karadzic will ask you a question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Could you tell us, please, this bullet point is saying that any activities directed at forceful expulsion is strictly banned, and that persons in the reception centre be treated humanely. Was that the policy of the municipal authorities?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes. If you need an explanation, I can add one. The policy of the municipal authorities in -- at no point in time used any pressure or force to get rid of the Muslim population. Instead, they tried to preserve law and order and prohibit any use of force.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Trial Chamber what you meant by item 4?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Municipal Staff is here -- just if you could blow it up a bit. I believe that it says it's activities --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. I mean paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes. The Bosanski Novi public security station, but I can't read the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And military police command.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: But can you put it back. The Bosanski Novi public security station and the military police command have been instructed to establish public law and order in Bosanski Novi under security of its inhabitants. According to me this is a logical position. We demand that the responsible services and institutions, of course within their power, exercise control of public law and order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. All right. The translation reads have been instructed, whereas the original can be interpreted as have been ordered.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, but you know, this is -- this all has a different dimension in this administrative document. It is all intertwined here. And then of course there's a question whether the one who's instructing is really competent to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But at any rate, an instruction on order is issued.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: But the Crisis Staff could not issue orders to the military police. However, the word used was often selected. It was often phrased that way to add more emphasise, although the recipient body was in a different line of hierarchy and reported to someone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said that you were present at many meetings of a regional character. Were you a member of the Crisis Staff of the RK Krajina, and did you attend its sessions?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, I was, but I didn't attend all sessions for purely technical reasons. At the time, it was sometimes even impossible to physically go to Banja Luka, and that's where the meetings took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And please try to be as brief as possible. Who did you represent at those meetings, and whose positions and decisions did you put forward? Did you represent --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: My positions, if there were any, were only on behalf of the Bosanski Novi municipality, and I must point out publicly, Mr. President, that unfortunately for technical reasons there was no communication with higher authorities so that I was angry at you sometimes maybe without justification, but there was very little subordination between the local level and the republican level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could all unnecessary microphones please be switched off.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
